title: ASIRT clears Edmonton police in 2015 death of man suffering psychotic drug episode
article: The province's police watchdog has cleared three Edmonton city police officers in the December 2015 in-custody death of a 49-year-old man.

Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) executive director Susan Hughson announced the results of the agency's investigation Monday, saying officers acted reasonably when they "repeatedly" deployed stun guns and restrained the man, who was wielding a large kitchen knife and in the grips of a drug-induced psychosis.

"It is clear that this man had the means to cause death and grievous bodily harm to anyone present in the residence, including himself," Hughson said. "It's also very clear, on all of the evidence, that the officers hoped to resolve this situation without serious harm to anyone."

Six officers were directly involved with the incident. Three used their Tasers, also known as conducted energy weapons, and were under ASIRT scrutiny.

Police were called to a home at the corner of 120 Avenue and 58 Street around 11:30 p.m. on Dec. 7, 2015. Officers encountered the agitated man, who was armed with a knife, when they entered the home. His teenage son also was home at the time.
After being shocked multiple times he was disarmed and restrained, and went into medical distress two minutes and 55 seconds later.
The man was given medical attention on scene before being transported to hospital, where he was declared deceased. Hughson would not identify the officers involved or the victim by name.

The chief medical examiner found the man died of "excited delirium syndrome" related to methamphetamine toxicity, ASIRT said. The struggle with police was considered "a significant contributory condition" in the death.

One of the first officers on the scene had dealt with the man six weeks before at a city casino, where he was reportedly high on drugs or having a mental breakdown. Police arrested the man under the Mental Health Act, but he was so strong, it took four officers to place him in handcuffs. He was later charged with assaulting a police officer and an EMS attendant.

On Dec. 7, the man arrived home from work around 6 p.m. He was in the house with his teenage son. Over the next five hours, he became increasingly paranoid and had delusions about his spouse, his neighbours, an imaginary intruder in the house and Satanic cults. The medical examiner found crystal meth in his system when he died.
Around 11:20, he called 911 and asked for the fire department to come to a neighbour's house. A neighbour called shortly after to report shouting and calls for help from the home.

Police smashed the glass in the front door, entered the home and found the man yelling and screaming incoherently with his son curled up against the cabinets on the kitchen floor. Police told the teenager to come toward them, which he did without interference. Officers tried to deescalate the situation - demanding the man to drop the knife - before firing their Tasers, Hughson said.
ASIRT has investigated 12 incidents involving conducted energy weapons, out of 442 total files. Seven resulted in death and five caused serious injury.
The agency was created in 2008 to investigate incidents involving Alberta police that result in serious injury or death, as well as allegations of police misconduct.
